'''''Eucalyptus eugenioides''''', commonly known as the '''thin-leaved stringybark''' or '''white stringybark''',<ref name="CANBR">{{cite web |title=''Eucalyptus eugenioides'' |url=https://apps.lucidcentral.org/euclid/text/entities/eucalyptus_eugenioides.htm |publisher=Euclid: Centre for Australian National Biodiversity Research |access-date=4 June 2020}}</ref> is a species of tree [[Endemism|endemic]] to eastern Australia. It is a small to medium-sized tree with rough stringy bark, lance-shaped to curved adult leaves, Flower buds in groups of between nine and fifteen, white flowers and hemispherical fruit.[[Image:Eucalyptus eugenioides buds.jpg|thumb|right|Flower buds]][[Image:Eucalyptus eugenioides fruit.jpg|thumb|right|Fruit]][[Image:Eucalyptus eugenioides.jpg|thumb|right|Specimen in the [[Australian National Botanic Gardens|ANBG]]]]

==Description==
''Eucalyptus eugenioides'' is a tree that typically grows to a height of {{cvt|25-30|m}} and forms a [[lignotuber]]. Its trunk is {{cvt|70|cm}} wide at [[Diameter at breast height|chest height]] and has rough, stringy, grey to reddish bark. Young plants and [[coppice]] regrowth have egg-shaped to lance-shaped leaves {{cvt|45-80|mm}} long and {{cvt|15-35|mm}} wide, glossy green on the upper surface and distinctly paler below. Adult leaves are more or less the same glossy green on both sides, lance-shaped to curved, {{cvt|70-160|mm}} long and {{cvt|9-35|mm}} wide on a [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]] {{cvt|6-20|mm}} long. The flower buds are arranged in leaf [[wikt:axil|axil]]s in groups of nine to fifteen, on an unbranched [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncle]] {{cvt|5-17|mm}} long, the individual buds on a [[Pedicel (botany)|pedicel]] {{cvt|1-5|mm}} long. Mature buds are green to yellow, oval to spindle-shaped, {{cvt|6-8|mm}} long and {{cvt|3-4|mm}} wide with a conical to beaked [[Operculum (botany)|operculum]]. Flowering occurs from July to January. The fruit is a woody, hemispherical or shortened spherical [[Capsule (botany)|capsule]] {{cvt|4-6|mm}} long and {{cvt|6-10|mm}} wide with the valves near rim level or slightly beyond.<ref name="CANBR" /><ref name="RBGS">{{cite web |last1=Hill |first1=Ken |title=''Eucalyptus eugenioides'' |url=http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Eucalyptus~eugenioides |publisher=Royal Botanic Garden Sydney |access-date=2 July 2019}}</ref><ref name="ABRS">{{cite web |last1=Chippendale |first1=George M. |title=''Eucalyptus eugenioides'' |url=https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Eucalyptus%20eugenioides |publisher=Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of the Environment and Energy, Canberra |access-date=2 July 2019}}</ref><ref name="Boland" />

==Taxonomy==
''Eucalyptus eugenioides'' was first formally described in 1827 by [[Kurt Polycarp Joachim Sprengel|Kurt Sprengel]] from an unpublished description by [[Franz Sieber]] and the description was published in Sprengel's book, ''Systema Vegetabilium''.<ref name=APNI>{{cite web|title=''Eucalyptus eugenioides''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/455947 |publisher=APNI|access-date=2 July 2019}}</ref><ref name="Spreng.">{{cite book |last1=Sprengel |first1=Kurt |title=Systema Vegetabilium (Volume 4) |date=1827 |publisher=Sumtibus Librariae Dieterichianae |location=New York |page=195 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/791550#page/787/mode/1up |access-date=2 July 2019}}</ref> The species name refers to its perceived similarity to trees of the genus ''[[Eugenia]]''.<ref name="CANBR" /><ref name="Boland">{{cite book|author1=Boland, Douglas J. |author2=Brooker, M. I. H. |author3=Chippendale, G. M. |author4=McDonald, Maurice William |title=Forest trees of Australia|publisher=CSIRO Publishing|location=Collingwood, Victoria|year=2006|pages=304|isbn=0-643-06969-0|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=CRQg11hSJ1kC&q=Eucalyptus+eugenioides&pg=PA304}}</ref> The term "stringybark" refers to the long, thin bark fibres that can be pulled off the tree trunk in strings.<ref name="anpsa">{{cite web|last=Walters|first=Brian|date=November 2009|title=ANPSA Plant Guide: Eucalyptus, Corymbia and Angophora - Background|url=http://anpsa.org.au/eucal1a.html|publisher=Australian Native Plants Society (Australia)|access-date=7 September 2011|archive-date=23 August 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110823222644/http://anpsa.org.au/eucal1a.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
The thin-leaved stringybark is found across eastern New South Wales from [[Wyndham, New South Wales|Wyndham]] north to the vicinity of [[Warwick, Queensland|Warwick]] in southeastern Queensland with scattered populations further north as far as [[Gladstone, Queensland|Gladstone]].<ref name="Boland"/><ref name="RBGS"/> It is a common tree of shale- and slate-derived, moderately fertile soils in lowlands and low hills. It grows in open forest with other trees such as grey box (''[[Eucalyptus moluccana|E. moluccana]]''), forest red gum (''[[Eucalyptus tereticornis|E. tereticornis]]''), cabbage gum (''[[Eucalyptus amplifolia|E. amplifolia]]''), manna gum (''[[Eucalyptus viminalis|E. viminalis]]''), woollybutt (''[[Eucalyptus longifolia|E. longifolia]]''), narrow-leaved ironbark (''[[Eucalyptus crebra|E. crebra]]''), and argyle apple (''[[Eucalyptus cinerea|E. cinerea]]''), spotted gum (''[[Corymbia maculata]]''), and with paperbark species such as prickly paperbark (''[[Melaleuca styphelioides]]'') and white feather honeymyrtle (''[[Melaleuca decora|M. decora]]'').<ref name="Boland"/><ref name=Ben98>{{cite journal|last=Benson |first=Doug |author2=McDougall, Lyn |year=1998 |title=Ecology of Sydney plant species:Part 6 Dicotyledon family Myrtaceae |journal=Cunninghamia |volume=5 |issue=4 |pages=809–987 |url=http://www.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0008/58049/Cun5Ben808.pdf |archive-url=http://webarchive.loc.gov/all/20090614173442/http://www.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0008/58049/Cun5Ben808.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-date=2009-06-14 }}</ref> The thin-leaved stringybark is one of the key [[Canopy (biology)|canopy]] species of the threatened [[Cumberland Plain#Ecology|Cumberland Plain Woodlands]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Cumberland Plain Woodlands|url=http://www.environment.gov.au/biodiversity/threatened/communities/cumberland-plains.html|access-date=7 September 2011|date=20 June 2011|author=((Department of Sustainability, Environment, Water, Population and Communities))|publisher=Australian Government|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110319195838/http://www.environment.gov.au/biodiversity/threatened/communities/cumberland-plains.html|archive-date=19 March 2011|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>Les Robinson - Field Guide to the Native Plants of Sydney, {{ISBN|978-0-7318-1211-0}} page 45</ref>

==Ecology==
The thin-leaved stringybark regenerates by regrowing from epicormic buds after bushfire and can live for more than a hundred years.<ref name=Ben98/> The [[longhorn beetle]] species ''[[Adrium artifex]]'' has been recorded from the thin-leaved stringybark.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Hawkeswood|first=Trevor J.|year=1993|title=Review of the biology, host plants and immature stages of the Australian Cerambycidae (Coleoptera). Part 2, Cerambycinae (Tribes Oemini, Cerambycini, Hesperophanini, Callidiopini, Neostenini, Aphanasiini, Phlyctaenodini, Tessarommatini and Piesarthrini|journal=Giornale Italiano di Entomologia|volume=6|pages=313–55|url=http://www.calodema.com/freefiles/176.pdf|access-date=2011-09-06|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120327223057/http://www.calodema.com/freefiles/176.pdf|archive-date=2012-03-27|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Cultivation==
''Eucalyptus eugenioides'' has been grown in California, where it grows best in coastal areas.<ref>{{cite book|last=McMinn|first=H.E.|author2=Mamo|title=Pacific Coast Trees|publisher=University of California Press|location=Berkeley, California|year=1969|orig-year=1937|pages=313|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ghyO_TcWZ1YC&q=Eucalyptus+eugenioides&pg=PA313}}</ref> In New South Wales, it is also known as "good kind stringybark" by beekeepers as the bees feeding on it are healthy and produce honey with a well-balanced amino-acid profile. It also provides the last crop of pollen before winter.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.honeybee.com.au/Library/pollen/eugenioides.html|title=Thin-leaf stringybark|year=2010|author=Honeybee Australis|work=Beekeeping in Australia|access-date=7 September 2011|archive-date=20 January 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120120014004/http://www.honeybee.com.au/Library/pollen/eugenioides.html|url-status=dead}}</ref><!--cites previous two sentences -->
